paragraphs: Since none of the regulatory texts examined requires a site to operate a quality system (Gap 1), Section 3.5 argued that the framework can be justified only by tracing each of its parts back to its origin. Sections 4.2 to 4.5 traced that origin instrument by instrument. A site deciding whether to adopt the framework would raise another objection, because it already keeps many records and a set of well-founded forms can still hold a problem that nobody reads. A site can note an unplanned component substitution in the operative note and again in the device accountability record, and the substitution can recur in later cases until a monitor finds it, since nobody at the site read the two records together. The framework therefore has to be justified as a whole. Its records have to connect, so that a record made in one place reaches a decision in another, and its parts have to be complete and necessary, with a control for every domain and an origin for every instrument. Table 4.3 lists the twenty-four instruments by pillar, with what each one reads and produces and the section and appendix where it is developed.

Information moves through the three levels of Figure 4.3, and each instrument works at one of them. At the lowest, a record holds the evidence of one event or one person, such as one procedure in the ICDL or the release of one person in the TRE. Above it, a synthesis reads several of these records together, such as the learning curve log for one surgeon or the follow-up review for one period. The decisions about how the site runs, from the delegation matrix to the risk register, are at the top and rest on those syntheses. Information rises through the levels, and a decision returns to the lowest one as the requirement that the next record is checked against. In a site that runs the full set, the substitution above takes this path. The ICDL records it in the operating room and the learning curve log reads it in the sequence of that surgeon's cases, so the indicator of surgeon procedural consistency can report it for the period. If the pattern holds, the PI records a decision in the POT, which may return the surgeon to proctoring through the credentialing record, and from then on the ICDL of that surgeon's cases is checked against the new condition. The event is therefore recorded under Operational Controls and decided under Governance, after being read under Risk Management and Performance Oversight, and for this reason the instruments were designed only after the functions of all four pillars had been defined.

Only five instruments ask for work at the clinical moment, the PSEAR, the ICDL, the IQL, the PFVR, and the SART, and they sit where Chapter 3 placed the data that cannot be recovered once lost. The other nineteen work on records that already exist, either those five or the clinical records of the site, so the set meets DR11 and the rule on source documentation. The same division explains why the minimum sets of Section 4.7 still close the loop. In a smaller set, the synthesis that a dedicated instrument would carry, such as the learning curve log or the indicators of the PIR, falls to the oversight meeting held under the POT. The records of the clinical moment stay at every level, four of them as instruments and the visit record through its proxy, so a site at a lower level gives up the dedicated reading of a signal and keeps the evidence that would show it. How much periodic work the nineteen represent for a small team has not been measured.

Figure 4.4 gives the justification that Section 3.5 asked for, since it crosses the twenty-four instruments with the twelve CtQ domains in its upper part and with the twelve design requirements in its lower part. A filled marker shows where an instrument carries the control of a domain or answers a requirement directly, and an open marker shows where it supports a control or an answer carried elsewhere. Across the full set, every domain has at least one filled marker, and so does every requirement that an instrument can answer on its own, so no domain is left to a general duty and no requirement is left without an instrument. Every column also has a filled marker in one of the two parts, so no instrument is in the set without a domain it controls or a requirement it answers. The training and credentialing records answer no requirement on their own and enter only through the control of domain 6, as the SIFSL and the PFVR enter through participant selection and follow-up. The PIR and the FUCR enter from the requirements, because an indicator shows whether a control worked without carrying it, as Section 4.5.1 states for eligibility, so their filled markers fall on DR8 alone. DR9 describes the set as a whole, as DR11 and DR12 do, so each of them runs across the lower part as one bar, and it is met by the phase that Figure 4.2 assigns to every instrument. DR11 and DR12 are met by the way the set is used, since the instruments work through the documentary system of the site and the minimum sets of Table 4.2 keep at every level the records that the regulations require.

The figure also separates the two kinds of control that Section 3.5 distinguished. Domains 5, 6, 8, and 9 rest wholly or partly on requirements that none of the regulatory texts examined assigns to the site. Their filled markers fall on instruments of the site's own, from the credentialing record and the learning curve log to the ICDL and the imaging records. Most of these directly answer the requirements that Section 3.5 derived from the four domains, so they are the controls that the framework adds to what the regulations ask of the site. In the other domains the filled markers fall mostly where the regulations already place a duty on the site, such as the delegation of tasks or the reporting of adverse events, so there the framework organizes work that the site already owes. Where it adds a control in these domains, the addition answers a requirement from Chapter 3, as the review of complications as a pattern answers DR8.

Consent rests on the eligibility record alone, because the regulations already set its process in detail and Chapter 3 gave it no requirement beyond the risk register, so its row holds a single filled marker. The control of endpoint assessment is thinner, since it rests on the visit record alone, which the follow-up review reads, while the qualification and consistency of the assessor, which the domain also covers, sit in the training records. When the endpoints of an investigation depend on readings that vary between observers, the site therefore adds the DTRM on the basis of its risk register, as Section 4.7 describes. The figures show that the records are designed to connect and that each part has an origin. However, no figure can show whether a site reads what it records in time to act, because that depends on the people who run the set and on the time they have.

Draft templates for all twenty-four instruments are in Appendices A to X. They were developed for shoulder device investigations, and their content reflects that context mostly in the complication categories and the imaging requirements, and also in the complexity levels of the learning curve log. Their structure, from the fields to the escalation logic, was kept as general as that context allowed, so adapting an instrument to another surgical specialty would in most cases mean changing its classification lists, although no such adaptation has been tested. The templates are provided in an open, editable format, so a site can match them to the layout of its own documents and add or remove fields, while the function that each instrument carries stays the same.
